clue.text: See 14 Down
Bored due to frequent exposure, ignoring large bottom

indicators.note: To ignore something is to take no notice of it, so one letter of the word just built is passed over and never reaches the grid.

parts.note: someone blasé is unimpressed because they have seen the thing far too often
large is L on any clothing label, and that L is the letter passed over

explanation.surface: Someone so used to the sight that even a large backside no longer registers.
explanation.walkthrough: Blasé keeps its accent in the dictionary and loses it in the grid, which is how a French import can hide inside four plain English squares.
explanation.definitionFit: The bottom of a thing is what it stands on — the same word does for the foot of a pillar or a lamp.

clue.text: Mount Everest's peak undergoes damage

indicators.note: A mountain's peak is its very top, and the top of a written name is the letter it starts with.

parts.note: to mar something is to damage it

indicators.note: Read it as two words: the letter goes under, which in a down entry means it is written below what came first.

parts.note: the first letter of the mountain's name, taken from its top

explanation.surface: The summit of Everest being battered and worn away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' wants to belong to Everest and is standing alone as the definition — a mare is a mount, and the mountain is only there for its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A female horse is something you ride, and any animal you ride is a mount.

clue.text: Victory when animal locked up runs off

parts.note: V for victory, Churchill's two fingers

indicators.note: Something locked up is shut inside something else, so the beast named goes inside the letters already laid down.

parts.note: 'as' does the work of 'when' in a sentence like 'as I arrived'
the animal is a moose, and it is the piece that gets shut in

explanation.surface: A caged animal bolting the moment somebody declares a victory.
explanation.walkthrough: An animal in a clue is usually anagram fodder or a hidden word; this one walks in whole and is simply surrounded by the two letters of a very short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to clear off in a hurry — American slang picked up from Spanish 'vamos' — and the -s matches 'runs'.

clue.text: Spanish guy departs

parts.note: one word for departing this life
and the everyday one — the clue's single verb is cashed a second time

explanation.surface: A man from Spain walking out.
explanation.walkthrough: One word of the clue has to be spent twice, once for each half of the name. Setters do this often and never signal it; the enumeration is what tells you a second helping is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the commonest Spanish men's names, so the definition points at a name rather than at a word meaning 'man'.

clue.text: See 19
Lovely place Surinam, occasionally Trump admitted

indicators.note: To admit a person is to let them in, so the piece just named is let inside the letters picked out.
Something done occasionally happens at intervals, and letters taken at intervals means every second one of the name.

parts.note: every second letter of the country, starting from the second
to trump a card is to top it

explanation.surface: A South American country letting a certain president in through the door now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' wants to be the president the surface is grinning about; it is the card-table verb. Surinam sits on the north-east shoulder of South America and is here purely for its spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The name for an imagined perfect society, which makes 'lovely place' a deliberate understatement rather than a straight synonym.

clue.text: One paying flying visit from Oregon best getting busy

indicators.note: Getting busy here is bustle rather than work: the letters mill about and none of them stays where it was printed.

parts.note: the state and the adjective hand over five letters each, and all ten are shaken

explanation.surface: Someone dropping in briefly, flying over from Oregon while everything gets hectic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying visit' does double duty in the definition: it is both the shortness of the stay and the literal way the bird turns up, which is what makes the definition fair rather than vague.
explanation.definitionFit: This small dark goose breeds in the Arctic and only drops in on British coasts for the winter — a visitor that arrives on the wing.

clue.text: He's not particularly concerned about upsetting celebs with intelligence

parts.note: gen is informal British for information or intelligence

indicators.note: upsetting in a down clue turns the word for about on its head, so it is read upwards

parts.note: re is Latin-derived crossword shorthand for about or concerning
the A-list is the group of top celebrities

explanation.surface: Someone indifferent to whether he offends famous people with what he knows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' turns RE (about) over to ER; GEN (intelligence) then ER then A-LIST (celebs), with 'with' simply joining.
explanation.definitionFit: A generalist has broad knowledge rather than a specialism, so he is not focused on any one particular field.

clue.text: Having conned rook inside, made oneself scarce

indicators.note: 'Inside' puts the letter named just before it within the previous word, and it doubles as where a con man ends up.

parts.note: to scam is to con, and the -ed answers 'having'
R is the chess rook

explanation.surface: A swindler who has taken somebody in and vanished before anyone notices.
explanation.walkthrough: Rook is a bird, a chess piece and a verb meaning to cheat. The clue leans on the chess sense for its letter and on the cheating sense for its story, and the bird is left out entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to clear off in a hurry, and its past tense answers 'made oneself scarce' with the tense already matching.

clue.text: Why 'noble' misrepresented royal

indicators.note: To misrepresent something is to set it out other than as it stands, which is what happens to these six letters.

parts.note: 'why' is the name of the letter Y, written down
the quotation marks flag the word as five letters rather than a meaning

explanation.surface: Somebody asking why a person of good character has been described unfairly.
explanation.walkthrough: Quotation marks round a word are a setter's nudge that it is being handled as raw material. The answer is a surname, which is why 'royal' can only point at a person by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry VIII's second queen, so the definition works by example: she was a royal rather than a word meaning royal.

clue.text: Attempts to prove wrong tense used in puzzle

indicators.note: 'Used in' sets the letter to work inside the other word rather than alongside it.

parts.note: a rebus is the sort of puzzle that spells a word out in pictures
T is the grammarian's tense

explanation.surface: A grammar question about which tense some puzzle is written in.
explanation.walkthrough: A rebus is the picture puzzle — an eye, a heart and a ewe for a valentine — and it is one of very few crossword words that names a rival kind of puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to argue that a claim is false; it stays an attempt because the argument can fail, and the -s matches a singular subject.

clue.text: Taking over in charge, monster emergin' — you bastard!

definitions.text: Taking over in charge, monster emergin' — you bastard!

indicators.note: A bastard version of anything is a mongrel, irregular form of it, so the letters come out mongrelised rather than in the order given.

parts.note: i/c is the standing shorthand for in charge
fourteen letters exactly as printed, the dropped g included
'you' throws its own three letters onto the pile

explanation.surface: A takeover, a monster surfacing and a shout of abuse at whoever is behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence describes the answer and supplies it at the same time, which is what makes it an all-in-one. The dropped g of 'emergin' is not just cockney colour: with it the letters would not fit.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole sentence reads straight as the picture: somebody has seized control, turned monstrous, and earned the shout that ends the clue.

clue.text: Angry tweet about empty fire extinguisher?

indicators.note: about tells us the rearranged tweet goes around the word for empty
angry suggests the letters of tweet are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
something blank is empty, like a blank page

explanation.surface: A furious social media post about an extinguisher that has run dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angry' rearranges TWEET to WET ET, and 'about' wraps those letters around BLANK. The question mark marks the definition as playful: a damp blanket smothers flames, and a wet blanket smothers fun.
explanation.definitionFit: A wet blanket is a killjoy who dampens enthusiasm, figuratively putting out the fire of a party.

clue.text: Expression of defiance suggested by nobles' wealth

indicators.note: suggested by says the answer is what gives rise to the following words when read as an instruction

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: its last word moved is an anagram signal, and the first four words rearranged give the letters of nobles wealth

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's riches prompt a defiant protest slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer is the instruction that would produce 'nobles' wealth', since WE SHALL NOT BE rearranged ('moved') spells NOBLES WEALTH.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a famous protest song and slogan declaring that the speakers will stand firm and refuse to yield.

clue.text: Method of selection for school team an asset

parts.note: a football or cricket side is eleven players, so a team is a number
an asset is a plus — something on the credit side

explanation.surface: Picking a school side, with one candidate having something extra going for them.
explanation.walkthrough: Selection is the hinge of the joke: the surface is picking a team and the answer is picking a school, and 'school' belongs to the definition rather than to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The exam English children sat at eleven, and passing it decided which secondary school they were sent to.

clue.text: Time for a party, I reflected

parts.note: per means for each or for a, as in ten pounds per head

indicators.note: reflected means shown back as in a mirror, so the word for party is read in reverse

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A party-goer musing that it's time for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflected' turns DO (party) round to OD, placed after PER and I.
explanation.definitionFit: A period is a stretch or span of time, such as a historical era or a lesson.

clue.text: See about including a little incentive — it should help things go smoothly

definitions.text: it should help things go smoothly

indicators.note: Turned about is turned round: the piece just named is written back to front.
To include something is to have it inside you, so the letter that follows goes within.

parts.note: lo! is the old word for see or behold

indicators.note: 'A little' of a word is a small piece of it, and one letter — the one it starts with — is as little as a piece gets.

parts.note: the first letter of the word, and nothing else of it

explanation.surface: Somebody slipping in a small sweetener to keep a deal running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lo' is the archaic word for see, met mainly in 'lo and behold' and in carols, and it is one of the handful of two-letter words a setter can build a three-letter entry from.
explanation.definitionFit: What you put on a hinge or a bearing so it moves without friction, and by extension what smooths any awkward piece of business.

clue.text: Commend school over accepting small number good at drawing

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the whole thing is turned upside down, read from bottom to top
accepting means the pair of words takes in the letter for number between them

parts.note: to cite someone is to commend them officially, as for bravery
a gam is a school of whales
N stands for number, here a small or abbreviated one

explanation.surface: Praising a school that takes in a few pupils who are talented artists.
explanation.walkthrough: CITE and GAM take N between them ('accepting') to give CITENGAM, and 'over' reverses all of it. A gam is a school of whales.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet is good at attracting, which is another sense of drawing, so the definition puns on art.

clue.text: With no time for a good wash, smell an irritation? Rubbish!

indicators.note: 'With no' says that something is missing from the word that follows, and what it names is what has to go.

parts.note: T is the standard letter for time, and it is the letter that goes missing
a good wash is a bath, three of whose letters survive
to hum is to smell, and never pleasantly — British and informal
a bug is something that keeps on irritating you

explanation.surface: Someone skipping a wash and being told, unkindly, how they smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark on the definition is the fairest signal in the clue: it says the answer is something a person shouts rather than a noun meaning junk.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrooge's snort dismisses whatever has just been said as nonsense, and 'Rubbish!' is the same exclamation in modern words.

clue.text: Right about sixth sense? Fools — they're wrong!

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the abbreviation for right is read backwards

parts.note: Rt is the abbreviation for right, as in Rt Hon
ESP, extrasensory perception, is the so-called sixth sense
asses are fools

explanation.surface: Mocking people who claim a sixth sense: they're fools and they're wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns RT round to TR, then ESP and ASSES follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespasses are sins or wrongdoings, as in the Lord's Prayer's forgive us our trespasses.

clue.text: Stick around, mate — Vlad's close to finish

indicators.note: around says the setter's letters and that final letter go round the word for mate

parts.note: Vlad is the setter, so Vlad's means I am, written I'M

indicators.note: to finish picks the letter that ends the word close

parts.note: the word close supplies its final letter
a pal is a mate or friend

explanation.surface: A friend is told to wait as the setter nears the end of his task.
explanation.walkthrough: Vlad is the setter, so 'Vlad's' gives I'M; 'to finish' takes E, the last letter of 'close'; and 'around' sets I'M...E around PAL. Fittingly, Vlad the Impaler shares the setter's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce or skewer something on a sharp point, which is one meaning of stick.

clue.text: Vital mail-order left inside by dock worker

indicators.note: inside places the letter for left within the rearranged mail
order means the letters of mail are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
a port is a place where ships dock
an ant is the classic crossword worker, from worker ants

explanation.surface: A docker leaves a mail-order package behind; it's vital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' rearranges MAIL to ALIM, and 'inside' puts L within it to give ALLIM; PORT and ANT follow, with 'by' just joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Something all-important is crucial or essential, so it is of the highest importance.

clue.text: Coach drops team leader for a start

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter out in front of the rest of it.
'For a start' says where that letter belongs — at the beginning, before anything else arrives.

parts.note: the letter at the front of 'team'
what falls in drops, taken as a noun

explanation.surface: A manager leaving the captain out of the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' looks like an instruction to delete something, which is the reading the surface is built to encourage. It is a noun, and what comes in drops is rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Coaching somebody is drilling them into shape, and the answer is the everyday verb for doing precisely that.

clue.text: Leaving, I wanted knighthood possibly?

indicators.note: 'Wanted' is the older sense of lacking, as in found wanting, so the letter it names is not there.

parts.note: leaving is going
the letter the word is lacking

explanation.surface: Somebody on their way out who had been hoping for a title.
explanation.walkthrough: Gong for a medal is the word a British paper reaches for at honours-list time, and 'possibly' is the setter conceding that a knighthood is only one kind of them.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal for a medal or decoration, and a knighthood is one instance of an honour — 'possibly' is what marks it as an example.

clue.text: Pub finally sacked crazy host

indicators.note: 'Finally' picks out the letter a word ends on, and nothing more of it.
Sacked is dismissed, so the letter just picked out is dismissed from the word that follows.

parts.note: barmy means crazy, and it is the word losing a letter
the last letter of 'Pub'

explanation.surface: A pub throwing out somebody who has been behaving oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: Barmy is British for crazy and comes from barm, the froth on fermenting beer, so the pub is still in the picture even after it has handed over its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A host in the older sense is a great armed multitude — the heavenly host — not the person who throws the party.

clue.text: African's principal relative a bit mixed up

indicators.note: 'A bit' keeps the shuffle small, and it is small: only the middle pair of letters actually change places.

parts.note: the principal reason for something is the key one
nan is a British child's word for a grandmother

explanation.surface: Somebody's chief relation, in a bit of a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' looks like the head teacher the school clues elsewhere have primed you for; it is the adjective, and the answer is a nationality rather than a person's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names the people of one African country, so the definition works by example: true of them, and true of many others too.

clue.text: He designs rubbish as well, I think

parts.note: tat is British for cheap worthless stuff — a stall full of tat
as well = too
er is the noise of somebody hesitating over what they think

explanation.surface: Somebody grumbling that a designer's work is junk, and hedging while they say it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is two words long and sits right at the front, which is the hardest place to spot it when the rest of the sentence runs on as naturally as this one does.
explanation.definitionFit: The man who draws the design and then inks it into the skin, so the definition names him by his trade.

clue.text: Offensive female's on moor

indicators.note: 'On' butts one piece straight up against the other, the female half laid against the offensive one.

parts.note: the Tet Offensive was the North Vietnamese campaign of 1968, named after the lunar new year
the female pronoun, straight from the clue

explanation.surface: An unpleasant woman out on the moors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' looks like the bleak upland the surface is standing on and is a verb here — what you do to a boat. 'Offensive' is a military noun, not an adjective about manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Mooring a boat is tying it up, and the answer is the verb for doing the same to an animal — the same rope, a different owner.

clue.text: See 12
